procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the High Court dated 17th September, 1975
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Court of Sessions acquitted the appellants. On appeal by the State, the Allahabad High Court set aside the order of acquittal and convicted the appellants under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, sentencing them to life imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court under section 2 of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act 1971 because the High Court had convicted them after an acquittal by the Court of Sessions. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the Court of Sessions' original acquittal.

directions: The judgment of the High Court dated 17th September, 1975 is set aside.
The judgment of the Court of Sessions is restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate court should be slow in disturbing the finding of fact of the trial court, and if two views are reasonably possible of the evidence on the record, it should not interfere simply because it feels that it would have taken a different view.

facts: The Sessions Court (the trial court) acquitted the accused after appraising the evidence.
The High Court (the appellate court) reversed the trial court's decision, setting aside the acquittal.
The case then came before the Supreme Court on appeal against the High Court's decision.
law: An appellate court should be slow to disturb a trial court's findings of fact.
If two views of the evidence are reasonably possible, the appellate court should not interfere simply because it would have taken a different view.
This deference is because the trial judge has the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses.
The initial presumption of innocence in favor of an accused person is strengthened by an acquittal from the trial court.
In an appeal against acquittal, if two views are possible, the view favorable to the accused should be taken.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the judgments of both the Sessions Court and the High Court.
It found that the conclusions reached by the Sessions Court were "fully justified," "plausible," and "possible" based on the evidence presented.
The Court noted that the Sessions Judge found the prosecution's evidence doubtful and committed no error in doing so.
It concluded that since the trial judge's finding was a reasonable one, the High Court should not have disturbed it, even if it was possible to reach a different conclusion.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in substituting its own conclusion for the plausible one drawn by the Sessions Judge.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the principle, holding that an appellate court should not overturn a trial court's finding of fact if it is a plausible and possible view of the evidence, even if the appellate court might have reached a different conclusion. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's decision and restoring the trial court's acquittal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the initial presumption of innocence in favour of the accused is weakened by his acquittal.

law.law_text: The initial presumption of innocence in favour of the accused is not weakened by his acquittal.
In appeals against acquittal, the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused must be especially kept in mind.
An appellate court should be slow in disturbing the finding of fact of the trial court.
If two views of the evidence are reasonably possible, the appellate court should not interfere simply because it feels that it would have taken a different view.

application.application_text: The Court established that an acquittal does not diminish the presumption of innocence; rather, it reinforces it. This strengthened presumption requires an appellate court to be highly deferential to the trial court's findings.
The Court reasoned that this deference is also due because the trial judge has the unique advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses testify.
Therefore, if the finding reached by the trial judge is a reasonable one, the appellate court should not disturb it, even if it is possible to reach a different conclusion from the same evidence.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that an acquittal weakens the presumption of innocence. Instead, it held that an acquittal reinforces this presumption. Consequently, an appellate court must be especially cautious when reviewing an acquittal and should not overturn the trial court's decision if its view of the evidence was a reasonable or possible one, as the initial presumption of innocence has been affirmed by the trial court's verdict.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellate court should be slow in disturbing the finding of fact of the trial court, and if two views are reasonably possible of the evidence on the record, it should not interfere simply because it feels that it would have taken a different view.
appellant_arguments: The conclusions reached by the Sessions Court (trial court) were fully justified and should not have been lightly set aside by the High Court.
The High Court was not justified in reaching a different conclusion, as the conclusion drawn by the Sessions Judge was a plausible and possible one based on the evidence.

The Sessions Judge correctly determined that the prosecution's evidence was too feeble to support a conviction and that the circumstances of the case cast doubt on the prosecution's version of events.
respondent_arguments: (Inferred) The High Court was correct to re-appraise the evidence and overturn the acquittal because the Sessions Court's assessment of the facts and witnesses was erroneous.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the initial presumption of innocence in favour of the accused is weakened by his acquittal.
appellant_arguments: (Inferred) The initial presumption of innocence is not weakened by an acquittal; on the contrary, it is strengthened, and an appellate court must give due weight to the trial court's finding.
respondent_arguments: (Inferred) The presumption of innocence is weakened upon acquittal, which allows an appellate court more latitude to review the evidence and overturn the trial court's decision.

statutes.act_name: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act 1971

cases.case_name: State of U.P. v. Samman Dass
cases.principle: An appellate court should not lightly set aside a trial court's order of acquittal when the conclusions of the trial court are fully justified and based on a reasonable assessment of the evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An appellate court should be slow in disturbing the finding of fact of the trial court, and if two views are reasonably possible of the evidence on the record, it should not interfere simply because it feels that it would have taken a different view. If the finding reached by the trial judge is not unreasonable, the appellate court should not disturb it, because the trial judge has the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses and the initial presumption of innocence in favour of the accused is not weakened by an acquittal.
obiter: The observation made by the High Court would be correct if Ajudhya and the two witnesses had really seen the occurrence. But if they were not on the scene of occurrence they might draw on their imagination and try to implicate persons on whom they had a suspicion.

The cumulative effect of the various circumstances enumerated above, in the opinion of the Sessions Judge, did throw doubt on the prosecution case and if the learned Sessions Judge in the circumstance did not think it safe to rely upon the evidence produced on behalf of the prosecution, he committed no error.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the trial court's acquittal because the conclusions drawn by the Sessions Judge were plausible and possible based on the evidence. An appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's finding of fact, particularly in an appeal against acquittal, simply because it feels it would have taken a different view, especially when two views are reasonably possible from the evidence on record.
legal_tests_applied: The appellate court should be slow in disturbing the finding of fact of the trial court.

If two views are reasonably possible of the evidence on the record, the appellate court should not interfere simply because it feels that it would have taken a different view if the case had been tried by it.

If the finding reached by the trial Judge cannot be said to be unreasonable, the Appellate Court should not disturb it even if it were possible to reach a different conclusion on the basis of the material on the record.
The initial presumption of innocence in favour of the accused is not weakened by his acquittal.
If two views of the matter are possible, a view favourable to the accused should be taken.
The accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt, which should be a reasonable doubt that a rational person would entertain.
policy_considerations: The trial judge has the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses, which places them in a better position to assess credibility than an appellate court reviewing a written record.
The initial presumption of innocence in favour of the accused is a foundational principle that must be kept in mind, and this presumption is not weakened by an acquittal by the trial court.
